themes.title: What heteroskedasticity breaks and what it does not

items.text: Unbiasedness needs only exogeneity E[u|X]=0, which still holds when error variance varies with the regressors, so the estimates themselves are fine.

The usual sigma^2(X'X)^-1 formula assumes homoskedasticity. With heteroskedasticity, t-tests and confidence intervals are invalid; in the spending example they tend to be too small, so the null is rejected too often.
Gauss-Markov requires homoskedasticity, so under heteroskedasticity OLS is not BLUE any more.
A funnel shape in the plot is the classic visual sign.
Regress squared residuals on the regressors; under the null of homoskedasticity, n times R^2 from that auxiliary regression is chi-squared with k degrees of freedom.
Same logic as Breusch-Pagan but the auxiliary regression also includes squares and cross-products of the regressors, so it catches non-linear forms at the cost of many degrees of freedom.
Keep OLS and replace sigma^2 X'X in the middle with the sum of squared residuals times x_i x_i'. Valid in large samples whatever the form of heteroskedasticity; the default in applied work.

items.anchor: Weighted least squares with known variance form
items.text: If Var(u_i|x_i)=sigma^2 h(x_i), divide each observation by sqrt(h(x_i)). The transformed model is homoskedastic and WLS is efficient.
Efficiency holds only asymptotically, and a wrong specification of h can hurt.
Taking logs of money variables often reduces heteroskedasticity.
In small samples robust standard errors can be biased downward, so HC2 or HC3 corrections are preferred. Cheap in large samples, so robust errors are a safe default there.

doubts.question: If the coefficients are still unbiased, why care?
doubts.resolution: Because inference is what gets reported; a wrong standard error can turn a noisy estimate into a significant one.

doubts.question: Should robust standard errors always be used?
doubts.resolution: In large samples they cost little; in small samples they can be biased downward, so HC2 or HC3 are preferred.

open_doubts: When exactly does WLS with an estimated variance function beat OLS with robust errors in practice?
